description: We are ITS TEAM, an award-winning technology team from Fırat University, Türkiye. With 2nd and 3rd place achievements at GakCoding Hackathon, we specialize in AI, software engineering, full-stack development, and UI/UX design. At NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to create innovative, impactful, and scientifically grounded solutions. We welcome passionate teammates skilled in AI, data science, space technologies, and research. Join us to turn ambitious ideas into reality!
summary:
ASTER is an offline-capable astronaut health research console built around a critical question: did the body change, the environment change, or the measurement become unreliable?

It connects three modules: breathing-phase-aware CO2 exposure estimation, sensor-contact integrity checks, and exercise-response comparisons under matched conditions. A local rule engine produces traceable events with data-quality labels, evidence, and review steps. When the evidence is insufficient, ASTER explains why it withholds an estimate.

During communication outages, the prototype continues local analysis and queues case packages for later delivery. Ground replies are linked to specific case revisions, so outdated advice can be identified.

The application includes 15 reproducible simulation scenarios, baseline comparisons, seven interface languages, and accessible light and dark views. NASA research informs its measurement assumptions and mission context. All physiological data are synthetic: ASTER is a research prototype, not a diagnostic or flight-qualified system. Our contribution is a testable workflow connecting measurement trust, contextual interpretation, and asynchronous crew-ground collaboration.
details:
THE PROBLEM

A changing health signal does not automatically mean a changing physiological condition. Local CO2 can include exhaled gas; a mechanical signal can change when a garment slips; and exercise responses can differ because the workload changed. Meanwhile, an intermittent or delayed ground link can leave crews without immediate support. A useful monitoring interface must make these distinctions visible before turning measurements into advice.

WHAT WE BUILT

ASTER is a working, simulation-first web application for the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.” It combines three research modules with a deterministic local rule engine, an evidence-linked case workflow, and asynchronous ground communication.

1. Breathing & Exposure

The software aligns simulated local CO2 measurements with respiratory timing and accounts for declared sensor delay. Users can inspect individual breaths and compare the candidate method with cabin, local-window, and phase-gated baselines. When sensor dynamics or signal quality do not support an estimate, the system withholds it and displays the reason. This is an experimental exposure estimate, not a diagnosis or a direct measurement of blood CO2.

2. Sensor Integrity

Simulated PVDF mechanical signals, motion, contact force, and reference excitation help evaluate whether a mechanical measurement remains interpretable. Contact and calibration checks gate downstream comparisons. A loosened sensor should trigger a measurement-quality review rather than automatically being interpreted as a physiological deterioration. Experimental compensation is kept separate from the released gating method.

3. Exercise & Muscle Response

Repetition detection and reference-session matching compare responses only when exercise conditions are sufficiently comparable. Load mismatch or invalid contact can cause the comparison to be withheld. Impedance is displayed as contextual evidence; it is not treated as a direct measurement of muscle mass. The system identifies experimental deviations, not muscle atrophy or fatigue diagnoses.

ONE EVENT, AN INSPECTABLE EXPLANATION

ASTER separates data origin, measurement quality, and interpretation status. Events retain the relevant time interval, rule version, supporting evidence, and next review step. Missing or stale inputs remain explicitly unavailable. Independent channels remain usable: in the combined scenario, a contact fault can withhold the muscle comparison without suppressing a valid environmental event.

WORKING THROUGH A DISCONNECTION

After the initial installation/cache, the browser prototype can run locally without an internet connection while its tab and device remain active. Case packages are stored in an outbox, retried, and deduplicated. Ground responses reference a specific case revision; a response to superseded evidence is marked as stale context. A separate local gateway and ground-process profile also demonstrates package exchange over real HTTP. The space-link delay is simulated: ASTER does not shorten signal propagation time or implement spacecraft radio infrastructure.

WHAT MAKES THE APPROACH DISTINCTIVE

The contribution we investigate is the combination of three explicit questions: is the measurement trustworthy, is the comparison meaningful, and does a remote response still refer to the current evidence? Refusing an unsupported interpretation is an inspectable outcome. The claim is not that wearables, dashboards, personal baselines, or store-and-forward communication are new. ASTER connects these established ideas to testable measurement-quality and comparison rules in a reproducible research workflow.

EVIDENCE AND LIMITS

The application provides 15 seeded scenarios covering nominal operation, local CO2 changes, exhalation contamination, slow sensors, contact slip, calibration mismatch, exercise changes, load mismatch, fluid shifts, link outages, duplicates, stale replies, malformed inputs, and storage failure. The analysis engine receives observations, not the simulator’s hidden truth; evaluation joins the two afterwards.

The included synthetic benchmark reports a candidate exposure MAE of 284 +/- 175 ppm, compared with 1250 ppm for the phase-gated baseline, 1259 ppm for the local-window baseline, and 1192 ppm for the cabin baseline across the stated scenario set. The candidate had the lowest error in 70% of runs. These results concern a simulator reference, not clinical accuracy. Negative findings are reported too: a fluid-shift-only scenario still caused an exercise-deviation event in 10% of runs. The full protocol, model assumptions, versions, and limitations are in docs/VALIDATION_REPORT.md.

NASA RESOURCES AND OTHER RESEARCH

NASA’s inspired-CO2 measurement work informed the distinction between nearby gas concentration and breathing-related exposure. NASA’s CO2 risk material, muscle-risk description, environmental and spacesuit references, and Human Research Roadmap provided mission context and scientific boundaries. CHP-IDSP and xEHR informed the integrated-data and asynchronous-review workflow. These are published research resources, not live astronaut telemetry, clinical training data, NASA-approved thresholds, or NASA validation of ASTER. Canadian Space Agency Bio-Monitor material and cited wearable-sensing research informed the prior-art review.

IMPLEMENTATION AND CURRENT BOUNDARIES

The interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and a PWA service worker. A Web Worker runs local processing; IndexedDB/Dexie stores browser state. Zod validates boundary data, Zustand manages UI state, i18next supports seven locales, and Motion provides reduced-motion-aware transitions. The local gateway/ground profile uses Node.js, Fastify, WebSocket, and SQLite. Automated unit, integration, browser, and accessibility checks are included.

CSV/NDJSON replay, WebSocket telemetry, and the serial reference-frame parser are emulator-verified only. External telemetry is validated but is not merged into the built-in simulated run. No physical sensor has been validated, Bluetooth LE is not implemented, and the optional camera feature is local preview only: no face, emotion, or medical inference is performed. All physiological data are synthetic and crew identities are fictional.

INTENDED IMPACT AND NEXT STEPS

ASTER aims to help crews and ground teams review evidence without hiding uncertainty, and to provide researchers with a reproducible environment for testing monitoring methods before deployment. Next steps are reference-instrument comparisons, physical-sensor testing, controlled human studies, and analogue-environment evaluation. It is a research prototype, not a medical device, flight-qualified system, or NASA-endorsed product.

AI ASSISTANCE DISCLOSURE

Yes. ChatGPT/Codex and Claude Code assisted with exploratory discussion, research assistance, requirements/specification drafting, code, tests, debugging, documentation, translations, presentations, and submission wording. The team supplied its initial wearable-sensing interests, selected the project scope, and directed the work. We do not present the development as unaided work or claim that all generated material has been independently validated.

The repository’s supplementary product film uses Higgsfield-generated narration (Qwen TTS), instrumental music (ElevenLabs Music), and one abstract video insert (Veo). The insert is identified as AI-generated; product-interface footage comes from the actual application. Media provenance is documented in deliverables/video/video-manifest.json and deliverables/video/README.md.

All physiological signals are synthetic outputs of the project simulator, whose implementation was AI-assisted; they are not astronaut recordings. Translations are machine-produced. Runtime interpretation is deterministic and rule-based, without a live LLM making medical decisions. AI assistance and scientific limitations are disclosed in the project materials.
